text: 287. Kal. kaḍí, kạí ‘gravy made from meat juices and flour’ is cognate with OIA (Suśr.) khaḍa-, khala- ‘buttermilk boiled with acid vegetables and spices’ (3783). Origin is unclear, but Mayrhofer (EWA) correctly refers to possible Dravidian origin; cf. e.g. Kan. kaḍi ‘curds mixed with salt, chillies, mustard, etc., and some rice flour boiled and seasoned’ (DEDR 1128).

text: 300. Kann. kár ‘sheep’, Rp. kar ‘ram; billy goat’, Bun. kar ‘sheep (male, castrated)’ — cf. Ind. kʌ́rū ‘lion, tiger; wild sheep’ with many parallels in languages in the northwest (loc.cit.); also Kann. byaṅ kar(h) ‘Tibetan ram’, Par. ɣarȭ ‘sheep’, Sak. kaura- ‘sheep’, Wkh. kar ‘mouton à courtes oreilles’, Bur. kíro ‘sheep (child’s language)’, karéelo ‘ram’, Sh.chil. kará̄ ‘a ram’ — Bhil. karᵃḍu and M. karaḍũ̄ both ‘kid’. As I have pointed out (2005: 103) the word might be of Dravidian origin, e.g., Tam. koṟi ‘sheep’ (cf. DEDR 1799 for Dravidian alloforms and semantic varieties similar to those of Northern Pakistan), whereas Harold Walter Bailey suggests derivation < PIE *kapro- ‘he-goat’ (1979: 65). But cf. also Čašule’s suggestion (e.g. 2010: 44) for a PIE background which he supports with reference to Bur. karóoỵo and Sh. karóovo ‘with curved horns’.

text: 67. Bng. tɔpkāṇɔ v.t. ‘to grope one’s way, grope along’ (with -k- and -a- suffixes), tɔprāḷ n.m. ‘groping step(s) that lead towards a goal’ (with -rāḷ suffix) and probably tɔpɔ n.m. ‘place or goal within reach, reach, range’, top(i)ṇɔ ‘to guess, figure, feel, touch’ (note topuiɔ pɔriaṇṇɔ ‘to make out or identify by touch or feeling’ [first verb is ABS, second < prájānāti ‘knows, understands’ 8509a]) and pɔrtɔpṇɔ ‘to feel around, grope about’ (with pɔr- prefix), Khaśdh. topiṇa and Deog. tōpṇɔ ‘to grope along’, Old Cam. tōpṇā ‘to look for’, Kann. taptapyá-mig (tap-ta-pyá-mig) ‘to touch, to search for by the touch, to feel or grope for, to seek by feeling’, Pāḍ. and Maṇḍ. tōpṇᵃ ‘to search’ — Ind. tʌ̀p-tʌpʰ karʌ́ṽ ‘to tap, touch lightly’, Bur./Sh. taptáp -̇t- ‘to tap on; tippen an’, and aspirated Ind. thʌ́p-thʌpʰ karʌ́ṽ ‘to grope or feel around in darkness’, Sh.chil. tháp-thap th- ‘to grope around in darkness’, Sh.koh. (RSup) thapȭ vakhat ‘evening’ (second word ← Ar. vaqt ‘time’), Bro. tʰʌptʰup ‘dark’. The aspirated Dard forms appear to be partly contaminated by OIA *thapp- ‘slap, pat’ (6091) – but note also Proto-Khasic *tʰaap ‘to hit, slap’ – whereas the unaspirated WPah. forms may have a parallel in Tam. tappu- ‘to grope, feel about’ (DEDR 2499). We are probably dealing here with a ‘North Indian’ word. Therefore see the following note: Note: A here perhaps related subgroup is this: Pur. ṭʰup ‘dark’ — cf. Bur. ṭumṭáṅ ‘darkness with (or through) dust’ if < older *ṭupṭáṅ (with second sylla- ble ṭaṅ ‘(sky) covered, cloudy, rainy’) — with Bur. are related Sant. ʈamɖao ‘to grope, to feel with hands or feet, as in the dark or in water, to search or try to find in the dark or in water’ (related with ʈamɖa ʈəmɖi ‘to grope, or feel here and there’ and Korwa ʈamɖaːo ‘to grope in the dark’ both of which possibly go back to older *ʈap-) and probably ʈahuʔp ʈaʈuʔp ‘stumbling, floundering, as one walking in the dark; to go slap dash’ (which might derive from older *ʈaʈuʔp ʈaʈuʔp).

text: 145. Ind. mʌ̀ṽ ‘a riverbank; a landing place, moorings (at a river bank)’, Kamd. gāl-mól ‘river-bank’, Wg. golmalˈa ‘river bank, valley floor’ (with first word < OIA *ghala- ‘stream’ [4453]), Dm. khoi-má̄li ‘river-bank’ (with first word < OIA *khola- ‘cavity, hollow’ [3943]), Paš. nandə-mālˈa ‘river-bank’ (with first word < OIA nadí̄- ‘river’) and vargamˈāl ‘river-bank’ (with varg(a) < OIA vá̄ri- ‘water, rain’ [11556]) — Orm. ṣʳī-mōl ‘field-embankment’. According to Morgenstierne and accepted by Turner, the Paš. and Dm. forms are < OIA má̄lā- ‘wreath, garland’ (10092). But this is implausi- ble. Therefore alternatively the words derive < PIE *molā ‘shore’ (Pokorny and Köbler but not Mallory and Adams; cf. e.g. Latv. mala ‘edge, bank, border, shore, region’), however contamination by forms related with H. etc. moṛ ‘curve’ (< OIA [ultimately Dravidian móṭati ‘twists’] is possible, cf. Kal. moḷ ‘turn, bend’). Note: See also somewhat similar OIA malaya- and Tam. malai ‘hill, mountain’ (DEDR 4742). Because of Dravidian and Indo-European evidence, Bomhald reconstructs PN *mal-a ‘hill, mountain (CINCL 846). Note, however, also In- scriptional Sanskrit māla- ‘field’ and lex. ‘a forest or wood near a village’, Munda Bodo-Gadaba mala ‘hill field, land cleared for ploughing’ and the synonym form mal biroŋ ‘mountain range’ with further parallels in Mon-Khmer like Brao məːl ‘dry paddy field’, Sapuan mɨəl ‘rice field (wet & dry)’, Tˈin mual ‘plant rice in hill field’.

text: 147. The following Bng. lemma has already been published (Zoller [1989: 195]), but here follows additional data: Bng. magu adj.,n.m. ‘a little but strong one (boy); a boy’ — Sh.ast. māgī ‘children’ (Nayyar [1986: 45]), cf. PIE *magʰus ‘young man’, but cf. also Sh. maági n.m. ‘darling (no sexual connotation)’ and PN *mag-a ‘young person, child; young’. Note, however, also Ta. maka ‘child, infant, young of animal, son or daughter, young age’ (DEDR 4616), Kan. maga ‘son, male person’, etc. Note: The genuine PIE origin of this ‘lemma’ has been questioned by several scholars, e.g. by Tatyana Mikhailova (2007: 16ff.) who postulates a merger of Nostratic *mVkV and PIE *maghu- ‘fellow, unmarried (p. 17), Ranko Matasović (2009 sub Proto-Celtic *makʷo- ‘son’) and Guus Kroonen (2013) who writes sub Proto-Germanic *magu- ‘boy, relative’ “[a] West European word of obscure origin.”
